title: Computer Networks and Distributed Systems
description: OSI, TCP/IP, routing, DNS and distributed systems theory

cards.q: Name the seven layers of the OSI model from bottom to top.
cards.a:
- **Physical**, the cable and the signal
- **Data link**, frames and MAC addresses
- **Network**, IP addresses and routing
- **Transport**, TCP and UDP
- **Session**, keeping a conversation open
- **Presentation**, encoding and encryption
- **Application**, what the program actually speaks

cards.q: Which OSI layer does logical addressing and routing?
cards.a: The Network layer, layer 3. It uses IP addresses and picks a path across networks.

cards.q: What is the difference between a switch and a router?
cards.a: A switch forwards frames using MAC addresses at layer 2. A router forwards packets using IP addresses at layer 3 and joins separate networks.

cards.q: How do the four TCP/IP layers map onto OSI?
cards.a: Network Access covers OSI 1 and 2, Internet covers 3, Transport covers 4, Application covers 5, 6 and 7.

cards.q: Name three things TCP gives you that UDP does not.
cards.a: Reliable delivery with acknowledgements and retransmission, ordered delivery using sequence numbers, and flow and congestion control.

cards.q: Describe the TCP three-way handshake.
cards.a: Client sends SYN with a sequence number. Server replies SYN-ACK. Client replies ACK. The connection is then open.

cards.q: Why would you choose UDP over TCP?
cards.a: When low delay matters more than losing the odd packet, such as live voice, video or games. Retransmission adds delay.

cards.q: What does the /24 mean in 192.168.1.0/24?
cards.a: The first 24 bits are the network part, leaving 8 bits for hosts. That is 256 addresses, 254 usable.

cards.q: What problem does NAT solve and what does it break?
cards.a: It lets many private hosts share one public IPv4 address. It breaks incoming connections, so you need port forwarding.

cards.q: Give two reasons IPv6 was introduced.
cards.a: 128-bit addresses remove the shortage, and the simpler fixed header with no router fragmentation speeds up forwarding.

cards.q: What happens when a resolver looks up a name from an empty cache?
cards.a: It asks a root server, gets referred to the TLD servers, then to the authoritative servers, which return the record. It then caches it for the TTL.

cards.q: Recursive versus iterative DNS query?
cards.a: Recursive means the server does all the work and returns a final answer. Iterative means each server returns a referral and the client follows the chain.

cards.q: Why is HTTP called stateless and how do sessions work anyway?
cards.a: Each request stands alone and the server remembers nothing. State is added on top with cookies, tokens or server-side sessions.

cards.q: What does TLS add to HTTP and when does it happen?
cards.a: Confidentiality, integrity and server authentication. The handshake runs after the TCP connection and before any HTTP data.

cards.q: Distance-vector versus link-state routing?
cards.a: Distance-vector routers share their table with neighbours and know only distance and direction, like RIP. Link-state routers flood link data, build a full map and run Dijkstra, like OSPF.

cards.q: What is the count-to-infinity problem?
cards.a: After a link fails, distance-vector routers keep learning stale routes from each other and the metric climbs. Split horizon with poison reverse and a low infinity value limit it.

cards.q: State the CAP theorem.
cards.a: A distributed store cannot have Consistency, Availability and Partition tolerance all at once. Since partitions happen, the real choice is consistency or availability.

cards.q: What does eventual consistency mean?
cards.a: If no new updates are made, all replicas end up with the same value. Reads can be stale in the meantime.

cards.q: Why can you not use a global clock to order events?
cards.a: Clocks drift and messages take different amounts of time. Logical clocks are used instead: Lamport for a partial order, vector clocks to spot concurrency.

cards.q: Describe two-phase commit and its weakness.
cards.a: Prepare phase: the coordinator asks everyone if they can commit and they vote. Commit phase: it tells them all to commit or abort. Weakness: if the coordinator dies after the votes, everyone blocks holding locks.

cards.q: What is a consensus algorithm like Raft for?
cards.a: Getting replicas to agree on the same ordered list of operations despite crashes. Raft splits it into leader election, log replication and safety, and needs a majority.

cards.q: Horizontal versus vertical scaling?
cards.a: Vertical adds power to one machine, simple but limited. Horizontal adds more machines, scales further and survives failures, but brings coordination and consistency problems.

cards.q: Bandwidth, throughput and latency, what is the difference?
cards.a: Bandwidth is the maximum rate of the link. Throughput is what you actually get. Latency is how long one bit takes to arrive.

cards.q: Why is packet switching more efficient than circuit switching?
cards.a: Circuit switching reserves capacity even when nothing is sent. Packet switching shares the link between many bursty flows, at the cost of variable delay.

cards.q: What is a man-in-the-middle attack and what stops it on the web?
cards.a: An attacker sits between two parties and relays or changes traffic. Certificate-based server authentication in TLS, checked against a trusted CA, stops it.

title: Theoretical Computer Science and Mathematical Logic

cards.q: What is an alphabet and what is a word over it?
cards.a: An alphabet is a finite non-empty set of symbols. A word is a finite sequence of those symbols, including the empty word.

cards.q: What does a deterministic finite automaton consist of?
cards.a: A finite set of states, an alphabet, a transition function, one start state and a set of accepting states.

cards.q: Are DFAs and NFAs equally powerful?
cards.a: Yes. Every NFA can be turned into a DFA by the subset construction, though the DFA can have up to 2^n states.

cards.q: What kinds of language does a finite automaton recognise?
cards.a: Exactly the regular languages, the same set described by regular expressions and by regular grammars.

cards.q: State the pumping lemma for regular languages and what it is for.
cards.a: For a regular language there is a length p such that any word of at least that length can be split xyz with y non-empty, |xy| at most p, and xy^i z in the language for all i. It is used to prove a language is not regular.

cards.q: Show the idea of why a^n b^n is not regular.
cards.a: A finite automaton has finitely many states, so it cannot count arbitrarily many a's to match the b's. The pumping lemma makes this precise.

cards.q: Name the four levels of the Chomsky hierarchy.
cards.a: Type 3 regular, type 2 context-free, type 1 context-sensitive, type 0 recursively enumerable.

cards.q: Which machine matches a context-free language?
cards.a: A pushdown automaton, which is a finite automaton with a stack.

cards.q: What does it mean for a grammar to be ambiguous?
cards.a: The same word has two different parse trees, so the structure and often the meaning is not unique.

cards.q: What are the parts of a Turing machine?
cards.a: An infinite tape, a read and write head, a finite set of states and a transition function that writes a symbol, moves left or right and changes state.

cards.q: What is the Church-Turing thesis?
cards.a: Anything that can be computed by an effective procedure can be computed by a Turing machine. It is a thesis, not a theorem, because 'effective procedure' is informal.

cards.q: Decidable versus semi-decidable?
cards.a: Decidable means a machine always halts with yes or no. Semi-decidable means it halts and says yes on members, but may run forever on non-members.

cards.q: State the halting problem and its answer.
cards.a: Given a program and an input, decide whether it halts. It is undecidable. The proof assumes such a decider exists and builds a program that contradicts it.

cards.q: What does it mean that a problem is NP-complete?
cards.a: It is in NP, and every problem in NP reduces to it in polynomial time. Solving one in polynomial time would solve them all.

cards.q: Give two NP-complete problems.
cards.a: SAT, the satisfiability of Boolean formulas, and the travelling salesman decision problem. Also graph colouring and the knapsack decision problem.

cards.q: What is the difference between P and NP?
cards.a: P is problems solvable in polynomial time. NP is problems whose answers can be checked in polynomial time. Whether they are equal is open.

cards.q: What is a truth table used for?
cards.a: Listing every combination of truth values for the variables to show the value of a formula, so you can see if it is a tautology, contradiction or satisfiable.

cards.q: What is conjunctive normal form?
cards.a: A conjunction of clauses, where each clause is a disjunction of literals. Every propositional formula can be rewritten into it.

cards.q: State De Morgan's laws.
cards.a: not (A and B) equals (not A) or (not B). not (A or B) equals (not A) and (not B).

cards.q: What does modus ponens say?
cards.a: If A implies B is true and A is true, then B is true.

cards.q: What do the quantifiers for all and there exists mean, and how do they negate?
cards.a: For all means the statement holds for every element, there exists means for at least one. Negating swaps them: not for all x P(x) equals there exists x with not P(x).

cards.q: What is the difference between syntax and semantics in logic?
cards.a: Syntax is which strings are well-formed formulas and which derivations are allowed. Semantics is what the formulas mean, which interpretations make them true.

cards.q: What is a proof by induction?
cards.a: Show the statement holds for a base case, then show that if it holds for n it holds for n+1. That gives it for all natural numbers from the base up.

cards.q: What does it mean that a proof system is sound and complete?
cards.a: Sound means everything you can derive is actually true. Complete means everything true can be derived.

cards.q: What does big O notation describe?
cards.a: An upper bound on how the running time or memory grows as the input grows, ignoring constants and small terms.

cards.q: Give the average and worst case of quicksort.
cards.a: Average O(n log n), worst case O(n squared) when the pivot is always the smallest or largest element.

cards.q: Why is mergesort O(n log n) in every case?
cards.a: It always halves the input, giving log n levels, and merging each level costs O(n). The split does not depend on the values.

cards.q: When is mergesort preferred over quicksort?
cards.a: When you need a guaranteed O(n log n), a stable sort, or you are sorting linked lists or data that does not fit in memory.

cards.q: What does it mean that a sort is stable?
cards.a: Records with equal keys keep their original relative order. Mergesort and insertion sort are stable, quicksort and heapsort are not.

cards.q: What is the complexity of binary search and what does it require?
cards.a: O(log n), and it requires the array to already be sorted and randomly accessible.

cards.q: What is the difference between an array and a linked list?
cards.a: An array has constant-time indexing but costly insertion in the middle. A linked list has cheap insertion once you are at the position, but you must walk it to find anything.

cards.q: How does a hash table work and what is the worst case?
cards.a: A hash function turns the key into an index. Average lookup is O(1). Worst case is O(n) when everything collides into one bucket.

cards.q: Name two ways of handling hash collisions.
cards.a: Chaining, where each bucket holds a list, and open addressing, where you probe for the next free slot.

cards.q: What is the defining property of a binary search tree?
cards.a: For every node, everything in the left subtree is smaller and everything in the right subtree is larger.

cards.q: Why do we need balanced trees like AVL or red-black?
cards.a: An unbalanced BST can degenerate into a list, making operations O(n). Balancing keeps the height at O(log n).

cards.q: What is a min heap and what is it used for?
cards.a: A complete binary tree where every parent is smaller than its children. It gives the minimum in O(1) and is used for priority queues and heapsort.

cards.q: Compare depth-first and breadth-first search.
cards.a: DFS follows one path as far as it goes using a stack or recursion. BFS explores level by level using a queue and finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph.

cards.q: What does Dijkstra's algorithm do and what is its limit?
cards.a: It finds the shortest paths from one source in a weighted graph. It does not work with negative edge weights.

cards.q: Which algorithm handles negative weights?
cards.a: Bellman-Ford. It is slower at O(V times E) but also detects negative cycles.

cards.q: What is dynamic programming?
cards.a: Breaking a problem into overlapping subproblems, solving each once and storing the answer, so you never recompute it. Fibonacci and knapsack are classic examples.

cards.q: What is the difference between memoisation and tabulation?
cards.a: Memoisation is top-down recursion that caches results. Tabulation is bottom-up, filling a table in order.

cards.q: What is a greedy algorithm and when does it fail?
cards.a: It takes the best local choice at each step. It fails when a locally best choice blocks the globally best one, for example the 0/1 knapsack problem.

cards.q: What is a trie and when would you use one?
cards.a: A tree where each edge is a character, so a path spells a word. Used for prefix lookups, autocomplete and dictionaries.

cards.q: What does Knuth-Morris-Pratt do better than naive matching?
cards.a: It precomputes a prefix table so that after a mismatch it never re-reads text it has already seen, giving O(n + m) instead of O(n times m).

cards.q: What is cyclomatic complexity?
cards.a: A count of independent paths through a program, computed as E minus N plus 2 on the control flow graph. It equals the number of regions in the graph.

cards.q: What is recursion and what must every recursive function have?
cards.a: A function that calls itself on a smaller input. It must have a base case that stops, otherwise it runs until the stack overflows.

cards.q: What does amortised complexity mean?
cards.a: The average cost per operation over a long sequence. A dynamic array's append is O(1) amortised even though the occasional resize is O(n).

cards.q: What is the difference between a stack and a queue?
cards.a: A stack is last in first out, a queue is first in first out.

title: Computer Architecture and Operating Systems
description: CPU, memory, processes, scheduling, file systems

cards.q: What are the parts of the von Neumann architecture?
cards.a: A CPU with control unit and ALU, memory holding both instructions and data, input and output, connected by buses.

cards.q: What is the von Neumann bottleneck?
cards.a: Instructions and data share one path between CPU and memory, so the CPU waits on memory. Caches and separate instruction and data paths reduce it.

cards.q: Describe the fetch-decode-execute cycle.
cards.a: Fetch the instruction at the program counter, decode what it means, execute it, then move the program counter on.

cards.q: What is pipelining and what breaks it?
cards.a: Overlapping the stages of several instructions so one finishes every cycle. Data, control and structural hazards stall it.

cards.q: Why do we have a memory hierarchy?
cards.a: Fast memory is expensive and small, cheap memory is slow and large. Registers, cache, RAM then disk trade speed against size and cost.

cards.q: What is a cache hit and a cache miss?
cards.a: A hit is when the data is already in the cache. A miss means fetching it from a slower level, which costs many more cycles.

cards.q: What is the difference between a process and a thread?
cards.a: A process has its own memory space. Threads live inside a process and share its memory, so switching between them is cheaper but they can interfere.

cards.q: What is a context switch?
cards.a: Saving the state of one process or thread and loading another so the CPU can run it. It costs time and is pure overhead.

cards.q: Name three CPU scheduling algorithms.
cards.a: First come first served, shortest job first, round robin. Also priority scheduling and multilevel feedback queues.

cards.q: What is starvation and how is it avoided?
cards.a: A process never gets the CPU because higher priority work keeps arriving. Ageing raises the priority of waiting processes over time.

cards.q: State the four conditions needed for deadlock.
cards.a:
- **Mutual exclusion**, a resource cannot be shared
- **Hold and wait**, you keep what you have while asking for more
- **No preemption**, nothing can be taken off you
- **Circular wait**, a loop of processes each waiting on the next

Break any one of them and deadlock cannot happen.

cards.q: What is a race condition?
cards.a: Two threads access shared data at the same time and the result depends on the timing. Fixed with locks, semaphores or other synchronisation.

cards.q: What is a semaphore?
cards.a: A counter with wait and signal operations used to control access to a resource. A binary semaphore acts like a lock.

cards.q: What is virtual memory for?
cards.a: It gives each process its own address space larger than physical RAM, using pages swapped to disk, and keeps processes isolated from each other.

cards.q: What is a page fault?
cards.a: The page a process needs is not in RAM, so the OS loads it from disk. Too many of these cause thrashing.

cards.q: Name two page replacement algorithms.
cards.a: Least recently used and first in first out. The optimal algorithm needs future knowledge so it is only a benchmark.

cards.q: What is the difference between internal and external fragmentation?
cards.a: Internal is wasted space inside an allocated block. External is free memory split into pieces too small to use.

cards.q: What does the kernel do and what is kernel mode?
cards.a: The kernel manages processes, memory, devices and file systems. Kernel mode allows privileged instructions that user mode cannot run.

cards.q: What is a system call?
cards.a: A controlled entry point from a user program into the kernel to ask for something like reading a file or creating a process.

cards.q: What does an inode store?
cards.a: The metadata of a file: size, permissions, timestamps, and pointers to the data blocks. The name lives in the directory, not the inode.

cards.q: What is RAID 1 and RAID 5?
cards.a: RAID 1 mirrors the same data on two disks. RAID 5 stripes data with distributed parity, so it survives one disk failing.

cards.q: What is DMA?
cards.a: Direct memory access, where a device transfers data to or from memory without the CPU copying every byte.

cards.q: What is the difference between an interrupt and polling?
cards.a: With polling the CPU keeps checking the device, wasting cycles. With interrupts the device signals the CPU when it is ready.

title: Database Modeling and Database Systems
description: ER modelling, normalisation, SQL and transactions

cards.q: What are the three parts of an ER model?
cards.a: Entities, the attributes that describe them, and the relationships between them.

cards.q: What is a primary key and what rules must it follow?
cards.a: The attribute or attributes that identify a row uniquely. It must be unique and never null.

cards.q: What is a foreign key?
cards.a: A column that points at the primary key of another table, which is how the relationship is enforced.

cards.q: How is a many-to-many relationship implemented?
cards.a: With a junction table holding a foreign key to each side, usually with both together as the primary key.

cards.q: What does first normal form require?
cards.a: Every field holds one atomic value, no repeating groups and no lists inside a column.

cards.q: What does second normal form require?
cards.a: First normal form, plus every non-key attribute depends on the whole primary key, not just part of a composite key.

cards.q: What does third normal form require?
cards.a: Second normal form, plus no non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute. No transitive dependencies.

cards.q: Why would you deliberately denormalise?
cards.a: To avoid expensive joins in a read-heavy system such as a data warehouse, accepting redundancy and update anomalies as the trade.

cards.q: What do the letters in ACID stand for?
cards.a: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.

cards.q: What does atomicity mean in practice?
cards.a: A transaction either happens completely or not at all. If it fails halfway it is rolled back.

cards.q: Name two problems that isolation levels prevent.
cards.a: Dirty reads, where you read uncommitted data, and non-repeatable reads or phantom reads, where the same query returns different rows.

cards.q: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
cards.a: WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters the groups after GROUP BY.

cards.q: What is the difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN?
cards.a: INNER JOIN returns only rows that match in both tables. LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table and fills in nulls where there is no match.

cards.q: What does an index do and what does it cost?
cards.a: It speeds up lookups on a column by keeping a sorted structure, usually a B-tree. It costs disk space and makes inserts and updates slower.

cards.q: What is a view?
cards.a: A stored query that behaves like a table. It simplifies complex queries and can restrict which columns a user sees.

cards.q: What is a stored procedure?
cards.a: SQL saved in the database and run by name. It reduces round trips and keeps logic close to the data.

cards.q: What is the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP?
cards.a: DELETE removes rows and can be filtered and rolled back. TRUNCATE empties the whole table quickly. DROP removes the table itself.

cards.q: What is a star schema?
cards.a: A data warehouse design with one central fact table holding measures, surrounded by denormalised dimension tables.

cards.q: What is the difference between OLTP and OLAP?
cards.a: OLTP handles many small transactions and is normalised for writing. OLAP handles large analytical queries and is shaped for reading.

cards.q: What is a NULL in SQL and why is it awkward?
cards.a: It means unknown, not zero or empty. Comparisons with it give unknown, so you must use IS NULL rather than equals.

cards.q: What is an SQL injection and how do you prevent it?
cards.a: User input is concatenated into a query and changes its meaning. Prevented with prepared statements and parameter binding, never string building.

cards.q: What does a transaction log do?
cards.a: Records every change before it is applied, so the database can recover to a consistent state after a crash.

cards.q: What is the difference between a clustered and a non-clustered index?
cards.a: A clustered index decides the physical order of the rows, so there can only be one. A non-clustered index is a separate structure pointing at rows.

cards.q: What is a service in ITIL terms?
cards.a: A means of delivering value to customers by helping them get outcomes they want, without them owning the specific costs and risks.

cards.q: What is the difference between an incident and a problem?
cards.a: An incident is an unplanned interruption or reduction in quality. A problem is the underlying cause of one or more incidents.

cards.q: What is the goal of incident management?
cards.a: Restore normal service as quickly as possible and limit the impact on the business, not to find the root cause.

cards.q: What is a known error?
cards.a: A problem with a documented root cause and a workaround, recorded so incidents can be resolved faster.

cards.q: What is a workaround?
cards.a: A temporary way of reducing or removing the impact of an incident when no permanent fix is available yet.

cards.q: What is the purpose of change management?
cards.a: To make changes in a controlled way so the risk of disruption is minimised, using assessment, authorisation and scheduling.

cards.q: What is a standard change?
cards.a: A low-risk, pre-authorised change that follows a documented procedure, so it does not need approval each time.

cards.q: What is an emergency change and how is it handled?
cards.a: A change that must happen immediately, usually to fix a major incident. It goes through a reduced approval path, often an emergency advisory board, and is documented afterwards.

cards.q: What is a CMDB?
cards.a: A configuration management database holding the configuration items and, importantly, the relationships between them.

cards.q: What is a configuration item?
cards.a: Any component that needs to be managed to deliver a service: hardware, software, documentation, even people or agreements.

cards.q: What is the difference between an SLA, an OLA and an underpinning contract?
cards.a: An SLA is with the customer. An OLA is between internal teams. An underpinning contract is with an external supplier.

cards.q: What is availability and how is it usually measured?
cards.a: The share of agreed service time that the service is usable, expressed as a percentage such as 99.9 percent.

cards.q: What do MTBF and MTRS mean?
cards.a: Mean time between failures, how reliable something is. Mean time to restore service, how quickly it comes back.

cards.q: What is capacity management for?
cards.a: Making sure there is enough capacity to meet agreed needs, at the right time and at a justifiable cost, now and in future.

cards.q: What is the service desk and what is its role?
cards.a: The single point of contact between users and IT. It owns incidents and service requests and keeps users informed.

cards.q: What is the difference between a service request and an incident?
cards.a: A service request is a normal user request such as a password reset or new equipment. An incident is something broken.

cards.q: What are the five stages of the ITIL v3 service lifecycle?
cards.a: Service strategy, service design, service transition, service operation, and continual service improvement.

cards.q: What is the purpose of a post-implementation review?
cards.a: To check after a change whether it achieved what was intended, had the expected impact, and what should be done differently next time.

cards.q: What is escalation and what are the two types?
cards.a: Passing an incident on when it cannot be resolved. Functional escalation goes to a more specialised team, hierarchical escalation goes up the management chain.

cards.q: What is a service catalogue?
cards.a: The part of the service portfolio visible to customers, listing services currently available with their details and how to request them.

cards.q: What is continual service improvement based on?
cards.a: Measuring, comparing against targets and improving in cycles, often described with the Deming Plan-Do-Check-Act loop.

cards.q: What is the difference between effectiveness and efficiency?
cards.a: Effectiveness is achieving the intended result. Efficiency is achieving it with the least resources.

title: Software Quality Assurance
description: Testing levels, techniques, verification and validation

cards.q: What is the difference between verification and validation?
cards.a: Verification asks are we building the product right, against the specification. Validation asks are we building the right product, against the user's real need.

cards.q: What is the difference between an error, a defect and a failure?
cards.a: A person makes an error, which puts a defect in the code, which may cause a failure when the code runs.

cards.q: Name the four classic test levels.
cards.a: Unit testing, integration testing, system testing and acceptance testing.

cards.q: What is black-box testing?
cards.a: Testing only against the specification, without looking at the code. Equivalence partitioning and boundary value analysis are black-box techniques.

cards.q: What is white-box testing?
cards.a: Testing based on the internal structure of the code, aiming to cover statements, branches or paths.

cards.q: What is equivalence partitioning?
cards.a: Splitting the input into groups that should behave the same and testing one value from each, because testing more adds little.

cards.q: What is boundary value analysis and why does it work?
cards.a: Testing values at and just around the edges of a range, because off-by-one mistakes cluster there.

cards.q: What is the difference between statement and branch coverage?
cards.a: Statement coverage runs every line at least once. Branch coverage requires every decision to be taken both true and false, which is stronger.

cards.q: Why is 100 percent coverage not the same as correctness?
cards.a: Coverage only says the code was executed, not that the result was checked or that the missing requirement was noticed.

cards.q: What is regression testing?
cards.a: Re-running existing tests after a change to make sure nothing that used to work has broken.

cards.q: What is a smoke test?
cards.a: A quick shallow test that the build starts and the main functions work, run before spending time on deeper testing.

cards.q: What is the difference between a stub and a driver?
cards.a: A stub stands in for a component that the code under test calls. A driver stands in for the component that calls the code under test.

cards.q: What is a mock object?
cards.a: A stand-in for a real dependency that also records how it was used, so the test can assert the interaction happened.

cards.q: What is test-driven development?
cards.a: Write a failing test, write the smallest code that passes it, then refactor. Repeat in short cycles.

cards.q: What does the test pyramid say?
cards.a: Have many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests and very few slow end-to-end tests. Inverting it makes the suite slow and brittle.

cards.q: What is static analysis?
cards.a: Examining code without running it, using reviews or tools, to find defects, style problems and security issues early.

cards.q: Why is a defect found late more expensive?
cards.a: Because more work is built on it. A requirements error found in production may mean redesign, recoding, retesting and released bad data.

cards.q: What is an exit criterion?
cards.a: The agreed condition for stopping testing, such as coverage reached, no open critical defects, all planned tests run.

cards.q: What is exploratory testing?
cards.a: Designing and running tests at the same time, using experience to follow up on what the system does. Good at finding what scripts miss.

cards.q: What is a code review and why is it effective?
cards.a: Another developer reads the change before it is merged. It catches defects, spreads knowledge and finds issues tests would not, such as unclear naming.

cards.q: What is the difference between quality assurance and quality control?
cards.a: Assurance is about the process, preventing defects. Control is about the product, detecting defects.

cards.q: What is a non-functional requirement and give three examples.
cards.a: A requirement about how the system behaves rather than what it does. Performance, security, usability, availability, maintainability.

title: Cryptography and Data Protection
description: Symmetric and asymmetric crypto, hashing, GDPR

cards.q: What is the difference between symmetric and asymmetric encryption?
cards.a: Symmetric uses one shared secret key and is fast. Asymmetric uses a public and private key pair and is slow but solves key distribution.

cards.q: Why does TLS use both kinds of encryption?
cards.a: Asymmetric during the handshake to authenticate and agree a key, then symmetric for the actual data because it is much faster.

cards.q: What three properties must a cryptographic hash function have?
cards.a: Preimage resistance, second preimage resistance and collision resistance. It must also be deterministic and fast.

cards.q: Why should you not use MD5 or SHA-1 today?
cards.a: Practical collisions have been found for both, so they no longer give collision resistance. Use SHA-256 or SHA-3.

cards.q: What is a salt and what attack does it stop?
cards.a: Random data added to a password before hashing, stored alongside it. It stops precomputed rainbow table attacks and means identical passwords hash differently.

cards.q: Why use bcrypt or scrypt rather than plain SHA-256 for passwords?
cards.a: They are deliberately slow and memory-hard, so brute forcing is expensive. A fast hash can be tried billions of times per second.

cards.q: What does a digital signature give you?
cards.a: Authenticity, integrity and non-repudiation. The sender signs a hash with their private key and anyone can verify it with the public key.

cards.q: What is a certificate authority for?
cards.a: It vouches that a public key really belongs to a named party by signing its certificate, so you only need to trust the CA rather than every site.

cards.q: What is the purpose of a nonce or initialisation vector?
cards.a: To make sure the same plaintext does not encrypt to the same ciphertext twice, which would leak patterns.

cards.q: Why is ECB mode a bad choice?
cards.a: It encrypts each block independently, so identical plaintext blocks give identical ciphertext blocks and the structure of the data shows through.

cards.q: What problem does Diffie-Hellman solve?
cards.a: Two parties agree a shared secret over a public channel without ever sending the secret itself.

cards.q: What is perfect forward secrecy?
cards.a: Session keys are not derived from the long-term private key, so stealing that key later does not let an attacker decrypt old recorded traffic.

cards.q: What are the three goals of the CIA triad?
cards.a: Confidentiality, integrity and availability.

cards.q: What is the difference between authentication and authorisation?
cards.a: Authentication proves who you are. Authorisation decides what you are allowed to do.

cards.q: What are the three authentication factors?
cards.a: Something you know, something you have, something you are.

cards.q: What is FIDO2 made of?
cards.a: WebAuthn, the browser API, and CTAP, the protocol between the browser and the authenticator. Together they allow passwordless public key login.

cards.q: Why is FIDO2 resistant to phishing?
cards.a: The key pair is bound to the site's origin, so a fake site cannot get a usable signature even if the user is fooled.

cards.q: What are the six lawful bases for processing under the GDPR?
cards.a: Consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, legitimate interests.

cards.q: What does data minimisation require?
cards.a: Only collect personal data that is adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary for the stated purpose.

cards.q: What is the difference between anonymisation and pseudonymisation?
cards.a: Anonymised data can no longer identify anyone and falls outside the GDPR. Pseudonymised data can be re-linked with extra information and is still personal data.

cards.q: What is the deadline for reporting a personal data breach under the GDPR?
cards.a: 72 hours to the supervisory authority after becoming aware, and without undue delay to the individuals if the risk to them is high.

cards.q: What does privacy by design mean?
cards.a: Data protection is built into the system from the start and by default, rather than added afterwards.

cards.q: What are the main activities of requirements engineering?
cards.a: Elicitation, analysis and negotiation, specification, validation, and management of changes.

cards.q: What is the difference between a functional and a non-functional requirement?
cards.a: Functional says what the system must do. Non-functional says how well, covering performance, security, usability and so on.

cards.q: Name four elicitation techniques.
cards.a: Interviews, workshops, observation, document analysis, questionnaires and prototyping.

cards.q: What makes a requirement testable?
cards.a: It is specific and measurable, so you can write a test that clearly passes or fails. 'Fast' is not testable, 'responds within 2 seconds' is.

cards.q: What is the standard user story format?
cards.a: As a role, I want a goal, so that I get a benefit.

cards.q: What do the INVEST criteria stand for?
cards.a: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable.

cards.q: What are acceptance criteria for?
cards.a: They define when a story is done, so the developer and the customer agree in advance what will be checked.

cards.q: What is a use case and what does it contain?
cards.a: A description of how an actor reaches a goal with the system, with a main success scenario, alternative flows and preconditions.

cards.q: What is the difference between a stakeholder and a user?
cards.a: A user works with the system. A stakeholder is anyone affected by it, which also covers management, regulators and support staff.

cards.q: What is requirements traceability?
cards.a: Being able to follow a requirement forwards to design, code and tests, and backwards to its source, so you can see the impact of a change.

cards.q: What is scope creep and how is it controlled?
cards.a: Requirements growing without corresponding time or budget. Controlled with a baseline, a change process and prioritisation.

cards.q: What does MoSCoW prioritisation mean?
cards.a: Must have, Should have, Could have, Won't have this time.

cards.q: Why are conflicting requirements a normal outcome?
cards.a: Different stakeholders want different things, and goals such as security and usability naturally pull against each other. They are resolved by negotiation.

cards.q: What is a prototype used for in requirements work?
cards.a: To make an abstract requirement concrete so stakeholders can react to something real, which surfaces misunderstandings early.

cards.q: What is the difference between validation and verification of requirements?
cards.a: Validation checks the requirements describe what the customer actually needs. Verification checks the specification is complete, consistent and unambiguous.

cards.q: What is a requirement baseline?
cards.a: An agreed and frozen version of the requirements that further changes are measured against and must be approved.

cards.q: Why is ambiguity in a requirement dangerous?
cards.a: Different readers build different things and nobody notices until testing or delivery, when it is expensive to fix.

cards.q: How does Design Thinking differ from classic requirements engineering?
cards.a: Design Thinking starts from user empathy and explores the problem space through iteration and prototypes. Requirements engineering focuses on capturing, specifying and managing agreed requirements.

cards.q: What role does the product owner play in Scrum?
cards.a: Owns the backlog, decides priorities and represents the stakeholders, so the team always knows what matters most.

cards.q: What is a definition of done?
cards.a: A shared checklist that applies to every item, such as coded, reviewed, tested and documented, so 'done' means the same thing every time.

cards.q: What is the difference between a population and a sample?
cards.a: The population is everyone you want to say something about. A sample is the subset you actually measure and use to infer.

cards.q: Name the four scales of measurement.
cards.a: Nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio.

cards.q: When is the median better than the mean?
cards.a: When the data is skewed or has outliers, because the median is not dragged by extreme values.

cards.q: What does the standard deviation tell you?
cards.a: How far the values typically lie from the mean. It is the square root of the variance and is in the same units as the data.

cards.q: Why divide by n minus 1 for a sample variance?
cards.a: Bessel's correction. Using the sample mean underestimates the spread, and n minus 1 makes the estimator unbiased.

cards.q: What is a quartile and what is the interquartile range?
cards.a: Quartiles cut the ordered data into four equal parts. The IQR is the third quartile minus the first, covering the middle half.

cards.q: What does a box plot show?
cards.a: The median, the quartiles, the whiskers up to 1.5 times the IQR, and any points beyond that as outliers.

cards.q: What does it mean that two events are independent?
cards.a: The probability of one does not change if the other happens, so P(A and B) equals P(A) times P(B).

cards.q: State Bayes' theorem in words.
cards.a: The probability of A given B equals the probability of B given A, times the probability of A, divided by the probability of B.

cards.q: When do you use a binomial distribution?
cards.a: A fixed number of independent trials, each with two outcomes and the same success probability, counting the successes.

cards.q: What are the key features of a normal distribution?
cards.a: Symmetric and bell shaped, defined by mean and standard deviation, with about 68, 95 and 99.7 percent within one, two and three standard deviations.

cards.q: What does the central limit theorem say?
cards.a: The distribution of the sample mean approaches a normal distribution as the sample grows, whatever the shape of the original population.

cards.q: What is a confidence interval?
cards.a: A range that would contain the true parameter in a stated share of repeated samples, commonly 95 percent. It is not the probability that this one interval is right.

cards.q: What is a null hypothesis?
cards.a: The default claim of no effect or no difference, which the test tries to find evidence against.

cards.q: What does a p-value actually mean?
cards.a: The probability of seeing data at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true. It is not the probability that the null is true.

cards.q: What is the difference between a type I and a type II error?
cards.a: Type I rejects a true null, a false positive. Type II fails to reject a false null, a false negative.

cards.q: What is statistical power?
cards.a: The probability of correctly rejecting a false null. It rises with sample size and effect size.

cards.q: What does a correlation coefficient of minus 0.9 tell you?
cards.a: A strong negative linear relationship, so as one goes up the other tends to go down. It says nothing about causation.

cards.q: Why does correlation not imply causation?
cards.a: The link may run the other way, be coincidence, or be driven by a third confounding variable.

cards.q: What is regression used for?
cards.a: Modelling how a dependent variable changes with one or more predictors, in order to explain the relationship or predict new values.

cards.q: What is the difference between absolute and relative frequency?
cards.a: Absolute frequency is the count. Relative frequency is that count divided by the total, so it is a proportion.

cards.q: What is a skewed distribution and where does the mean sit?
cards.a: One tail is longer. In a right skew the mean is pulled above the median, in a left skew below it.
